signals.title: When Certificates Fail: A Unified Safety Framework for Embedded Neural Interface Models
signals.summary: Formal robustness certificates for embedded neural-interface models can pass while task accuracy collapses: at perturbation budget e=0.25, EEGNet classification accuracy drops by 25.7% under projected-gradient attack while the Lipschitz-style certificate remains valid for all 9 tested subjects. We argue that this gap between mathematical certification and operational safety is one instance of a broader alignment failure in neural interfaces, where training objectives diverge from user welfare.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators. High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: Formal robustness certificates for embedded neural-interface models can remain valid even when the accuracy of tasks, such as EEGNet classification, significantly declines under certain attacks. Specifically, with a perturbation budget of e=0.25, the accuracy drops by 25.7%, while the Lipschitz-style certificate continues to hold for all tested subjects. This discrepancy between mathematical certification and operational safety highlights a larger issue of misalignment in neural interfaces, where training goals do not align with user welfare. Understanding this gap is critical for developing safer AI systems that truly serve user interests rather than just passing technical evaluations. This is particularly relevant for the community as it underscores the importance of critically assessing the efficacy and safety of AI models beyond their theoretical certifications.

signals.title: DiaLLM: An Investigation into the Robustness-Generation Gap in English Dialect Adaptation
signals.summary: Large language models increasingly \emph{understand} dialectal English, yet still \emph{produce} only standard, US-leaning English, leaving dialectal generation, the harder half of the problem, largely unaddressed. We introduce \textbf{DiaLLM}, which continually pretrains three open-weight language model families on the International Corpus of English and applies implicit and explicit post-training paradigms, each combined with three model alignment strategies, giving the first controlled comparison of these components across Australian, Indian, and Northern British English.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators. Monitor adoption pressure and revise formation cadence for tool onboarding.
signals.long_summary: Large language models have shown progress in understanding dialectal English, but they still predominantly generate standard, US-centric English. The study introduces DiaLLM, which aims to address this gap by continuously pretraining three families of open-weight language models using the International Corpus of English. The research employs both implicit and explicit post-training methods in conjunction with three alignment strategies, offering a controlled comparison across various English dialects, specifically Australian, Indian, and Northern British English. This investigation highlights the challenges in dialectal generation and aims to enhance language model adaptability to diverse English dialects. Understanding advancements like DiaLLM is crucial for the community to recognize ongoing efforts in making AI linguistically inclusive and versatile.
